questions.q: A 25-year-old male with multibacillary leprosy on WHO-MDT for 6 months presents with sudden painful erythematous swelling of existing skin lesions, fever of 38.8°C, and new nerve tenderness. No new lesions are present. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Stop MDT immediately and start prednisolone 40 mg/day
Continue MDT and add prednisolone 40 mg/day
Stop MDT and start thalidomide 100 mg/day
Switch to second-line MDT regimen and add clofazimine
questions.exp: Type 1 (reversal) lepra reaction requires continuation of MDT — stopping MDT is dangerous and incorrect. Prednisolone 40 mg/day (tapering over 12-24 weeks) is added to control immune-mediated inflammation and prevent nerve damage.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with painful oral erosions for 3 months followed by flaccid blisters on the trunk that rupture easily, leaving raw areas. Nikolsky sign is positive. Which autoantibody is primarily responsible for mucosal involvement in this condition?
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris with mucosal involvement is mediated primarily by anti-Dsg3 antibodies. Dsg3 is the predominant adhesion molecule in mucosae. Anti-Dsg1 alone causes pemphigus foliaceus (no mucosal involvement). Combined anti-Dsg1+Dsg3 causes mucocutaneous PV.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male presents with a pigmented lesion on his back (asymmetry, irregular border, mixed colours, diameter 9 mm). Wide excision confirms melanoma. Which single factor most strongly determines his 5-year survival prognosis?
questions.exp: Breslow thickness (depth of invasion in mm) is the single most important prognostic factor in primary melanoma and directly determines T-staging in AJCC 8th edition. Clark level has been removed from current staging due to lesser prognostic weight.

questions.q: A 30-year-old farmer presents with circular erythematous scaly patches on the groin with central clearing and an active advancing border. KOH mount confirms dermatophyte infection. Which organism is most commonly responsible for tinea cruris in India?
questions.exp: Trichophyton rubrum is the most common dermatophyte causing tinea cruris, tinea pedis, and tinea unguium worldwide and in India. T. mentagrophytes is second most common. M. canis primarily causes tinea capitis and tinea corporis acquired from animals.

questions.q: A 28-year-old sexually active male presents with a single painless indurated ulcer on the glans penis for 10 days. Dark-field microscopy confirms motile spirochetes. VDRL is reactive at 1:4 and TPHA is positive. What is the drug of choice?
opts: Doxycycline 100 mg BD orally for 14 days
Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose
Ceftriaxone 1 g IM daily for 10 days
questions.exp: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose remains the drug of choice for primary syphilis. Doxycycline for 14 days is the preferred alternative in penicillin-allergic patients. Azithromycin has emerging resistance and is no longer recommended as primary therapy.

questions.q: A 70-year-old male presents with intensely pruritic tense blisters on an urticarial base on the trunk and flexures. Nikolsky sign is negative. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 deposition at the dermal-epidermal junction. The target antigens are:
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid is characterised by IgG autoantibodies against BP180 (NC16A domain of collagen XVII, the transmembrane hemidesmosomal protein) and BP230 (intracellular hemidesmosomal plaque protein). Linear IgG+C3 at DEJ is classic. Tense blisters (subepidermal) differ from flaccid (intraepidermal) pemphigus blisters.

questions.q: A 35-year-old presents with 4 well-defined hypopigmented patches with clear-cut sensory loss. No peripheral nerve thickening is found. Slit skin smear is negative (BI = 0). According to WHO operational classification, this patient should be treated as:
opts: Pure neuritic leprosy — ROM single-dose therapy
questions.exp: WHO operational classification: PB leprosy = 1-5 skin lesions with negative SSS. MB leprosy = 6+ skin lesions OR positive SSS. This patient has 4 lesions and negative SSS — paucibacillary leprosy, treated with 6-month MDT-PB (rifampicin + dapsone).

questions.q: A 25-year-old female on phenytoin for epilepsy develops fever, morbilliform rash, bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy, and hepatitis 6 weeks after starting the drug. CBC shows eosinophilia (1,800 cells/µL). What is the diagnosis?
opts: Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms (DRESS)
questions.exp: DRESS presents 2-8 weeks after drug initiation with fever, morbilliform eruption, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, and visceral organ involvement. Aromatic anticonvulsants (phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbitone) are classic triggers. Mortality is ~10% without prompt management. RegiSCAR criteria used for diagnosis.

questions.q: A patient with severe plaque psoriasis is started on a biologic that targets the shared p40 subunit of IL-12 and IL-23, thereby inhibiting both Th1 and Th17 pathways. Which drug is this?
questions.exp: Ustekinumab is a human monoclonal antibody targeting the p40 subunit shared by IL-12 and IL-23, inhibiting both Th1 (via IL-12) and Th17 (via IL-23) pathways. Secukinumab and ixekizumab target IL-17A. Guselkumab targets IL-23 p19 subunit specifically.

questions.q: During dermoscopy of a skin-coloured papule on an elderly patient's cheek, the dermatologist identifies leaf-like grey-brown areas, spoke-wheel pattern, and large blue-grey ovoid nests. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Leaf-like areas, spoke-wheel structures, and blue-grey ovoid nests are specific dermoscopic criteria for pigmented basal cell carcinoma. Seborrhoeic keratosis shows milia-like cysts and comedo-like openings. Dermatofibroma shows central white scar-like patch with peripheral pigment network.

questions.q: A 19-year-old female presents with moderate acne vulgaris showing numerous open and closed comedones, fewer than 20 inflammatory papules, and no nodules or cysts. The most appropriate first-line treatment is:
questions.exp: For moderate predominantly comedonal acne, combination of topical retinoid (adapalene normalises follicular keratinisation) plus benzoyl peroxide (antimicrobial, prevents antibiotic resistance) is the evidence-based first-line treatment. Oral antibiotics require a topical retinoid partner. Isotretinoin is reserved for severe/nodulocystic acne or failure of standard therapy.

questions.q: A 22-year-old presents with multiple hypo- and hyperpigmented macules on the trunk with fine branny scaling. KOH preparation shows a 'spaghetti and meatballs' pattern. The primary causative species is:
questions.exp: Pityriasis (tinea) versicolor is caused by Malassezia species, predominantly M. globosa and M. furfur. KOH shows short hyphae and round yeast cells resembling 'spaghetti and meatballs'. Piedraia hortae causes black piedra; Trichophyton causes dermatophytosis.

questions.q: A 25-year-old female presents with butterfly rash, photosensitivity, arthralgia, and alopecia. ANA titre is 1:640 (speckled), anti-dsDNA is elevated, and C3/C4 are low. Which autoantibody is considered most SPECIFIC for SLE?
questions.exp: Anti-Sm (Smith) antibodies are the most specific for SLE (>99% specificity) though sensitivity is only 25-30%. Anti-dsDNA is more sensitive and correlates with disease activity/nephritis but is less specific. Anti-histone antibodies are characteristic of drug-induced lupus. Anti-Ro/SSA is associated with neonatal lupus and Sjogren syndrome.

questions.q: A 30-year-old with lepromatous leprosy on MDT presents with crops of painful, tender erythematous nodules on the face and extremities, fever of 39°C, arthralgia, and iridocyclitis. The drug of choice for this reaction is:
questions.exp: Erythema nodosum leprosum (Type 2 lepra reaction) in lepromatous leprosy is best treated with thalidomide (100-300 mg/day) — it is the most effective agent and drug of choice in males and post-menopausal women (teratogenic, contraindicated in women of reproductive age). MDT must always be continued. Steroids are used when thalidomide is contraindicated.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with pruritic violaceous flat-topped polygonal papules on the flexor wrists and ankles, with white lacy lines on buccal mucosa. Skin biopsy is performed. Which histopathological combination is pathognomonic of this condition?
opts: Hypergranulosis, sawtooth rete ridges, and band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at DEJ
questions.exp: Lichen planus histology: wedge-shaped hypergranulosis, irregular acanthosis with sawtooth rete ridges, band-like lymphohistiocytic infiltrate hugging the DEJ (lichenoid infiltrate), squamatisation of basal layer, and Civatte (colloid/cytoid) bodies. This triad is pathognomonic.

questions.q: A neonate born to an untreated VDRL-positive mother presents with snuffles, hepatosplenomegaly, and a maculopapular rash on palms and soles. X-ray of the tibia shows bilateral symmetrical destruction of the medial proximal tibial metaphyses. This radiological sign is called:
questions.exp: Wimberger sign refers to bilateral symmetrical destruction (lytic lesions) of the medial proximal tibial metaphyses, pathognomonic of congenital syphilis. Parrot's pseudoparalysis results from periostitis causing pain on movement. Both are features of early congenital syphilis.

questions.q: A 10-year-old child with 3 weeks of intense nocturnal pruritus has several affected family members. Examination reveals linear burrows between fingers, papules on the scrotum, and excoriations. Scabies is confirmed on microscopy. The drug of choice for treatment is:
opts: Benzyl benzoate 25% — applied for 3 consecutive nights
questions.exp: Permethrin 5% cream is the drug of choice for scabies in children >2 months and adults. Applied overnight to the whole body below the neck and washed off after 8-12 hours. A second application 1 week later is recommended. Lindane is neurotoxic and contraindicated in children. Ivermectin is effective but not first-line in children <15 kg.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with proximal muscle weakness, heliotrope rash, Gottron's papules, V-sign, and shawl sign. CK is markedly elevated. After confirming dermatomyositis, what is the most important next investigation?
opts: CT scan of chest, abdomen, and pelvis to screen for occult malignancy
questions.exp: Adult dermatomyositis carries a 15-30% risk of underlying malignancy (ovarian, lung, gastric, colorectal, breast, nasopharyngeal — particularly in Asian patients). Screening with CT of chest/abdomen/pelvis (+ mammography, pelvic US, colonoscopy as indicated) is the most critical initial step after diagnosis confirmation.

questions.q: A 22-year-old female with severe nodulocystic acne is prescribed oral isotretinoin. She is counselled about teratogenicity. Which pattern of birth defects constitutes 'retinoid embryopathy'?
opts: CNS abnormalities, craniofacial defects, and conotruncal cardiac defects
questions.exp: Retinoid (isotretinoin) embryopathy affects structures derived from cephalic neural crest cells: CNS (hydrocephalus, cerebellar vermis agenesis), craniofacial (microtia/anotia, cleft palate, micrognathia), and cardiovascular (conotruncal defects — transposition of great arteries, VSD). Exposure is most dangerous in the first trimester. Two forms of contraception are mandatory (iPLEDGE protocol).

questions.q: A 28-year-old presents with stable segmental vitiligo on the right cheek for 2 years with no new lesion activity. Surgical intervention is planned. Which procedure offers the best repigmentation for a large stable vitiligo lesion?
questions.exp: MKTP (non-cultured epidermal suspension transplantation) provides the best cosmetic outcome for large areas of stable vitiligo, covering up to 10x the donor site area. Suction blister grafting is excellent for small areas with superior cosmetic results. Punch grafting is used for small focal areas but risks cobblestone scarring. All require disease stability for at least 1-2 years.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman presents with superficial flaccid blisters that rupture easily, leaving crusted erosions on the scalp, face, and seborrhoeic areas of the chest and back. Mucous membranes are completely spared. The target autoantigen is:
questions.exp: Pemphigus foliaceus targets Dsg1, expressed predominantly in the superficial epidermis and absent in mucosae. Dsg3 (expressed in all mucosal epithelia) compensates in mucosae, explaining the absence of oral lesions. In PV with mucosal involvement, anti-Dsg3 predominates. Endemic form of PF (Fogo selvagem) is prevalent in Brazil.

questions.q: A 24-year-old male presents with a 5-day history of profuse purulent urethral discharge and dysuria. Gram stain of urethral exudate shows gram-negative intracellular diplococci. As per current WHO 2023 guidelines, the recommended treatment is:
questions.exp: Due to widespread fluoroquinolone resistance, ciprofloxacin is no longer recommended. Ceftriaxone 500 mg (or 1 g if pharyngeal infection) IM single dose is now the monotherapy of choice for uncomplicated gonorrhoea per updated WHO/CDC guidelines. Co-administration of azithromycin is no longer routinely recommended due to emerging dual resistance.

questions.q: A 65-year-old male has a biopsy-confirmed BCC on the nose. Which histological subtype carries the highest recurrence rate and worst prognosis?
questions.exp: Morpheaform (sclerosing/fibrosing) BCC is the most aggressive subtype with ill-defined clinical margins, deeply infiltrating fibrous stroma, and the highest recurrence rate (up to 50% with standard excision). It requires Mohs micrographic surgery. Nodular BCC is the most common (60-70%) but has a much better prognosis. Superficial BCC is the least aggressive.

questions.q: A 50-year-old diabetic male presents with yellowish, thickened, crumbling toenails with subungual debris, confirmed as dermatophyte onychomycosis on KOH and culture. The most effective systemic treatment regimen is:
opts: Itraconazole pulse (400 mg/day for 1 week/month for 3 pulses)
questions.exp: Terbinafine 250 mg daily for 12 weeks (toenails) or 6 weeks (fingernails) is the most effective treatment for dermatophyte onychomycosis, with mycological cure rates of 70-80%. It is fungicidal against dermatophytes. Itraconazole pulse is fungistatic but preferred for non-dermatophyte moulds. Griseofulvin has low cure rates for onychomycosis.

questions.q: A 28-year-old male presents with a painless genital ulcer that healed spontaneously 3 weeks ago, now followed by tender unilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy. Examination shows the lymphadenopathy is divided by the inguinal ligament (groove sign). What is the causative organism and drug of choice?
opts: Haemophilus ducreyi — azithromycin 1 g single dose
Chlamydia trachomatis (serovars L1-L3) — doxycycline 100 mg BD for 21 days
Treponema pallidum — benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU IM
Klebsiella granulomatis — doxycycline 100 mg BD for 3 weeks
questions.exp: Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) is caused by C. trachomatis serovars L1, L2, L2b, L3. The groove sign (inguinal adenopathy bisected by Poupart's ligament) is pathognomonic. Treatment: doxycycline 100 mg BD for 21 days. Azithromycin 1 g weekly x 3 is an alternative. Klebsiella granulomatis causes donovanosis (granuloma inguinale).

questions.q: A 42-year-old male with plaque psoriasis of 10 years has nail changes. Dermoscopy reveals yellow-orange discolouration visible through the nail plate (oil-drop appearance). Which nail change in psoriasis is considered MOST SPECIFIC?
questions.exp: The oil drop (salmon patch) sign — yellow-orange translucent discolouration under the nail plate representing dermal inflammation — is the most specific psoriatic nail change. Pitting is the most common but also occurs in alopecia areata and eczema. Onycholysis and subungual hyperkeratosis are frequent but non-specific.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis on hydroxychloroquine for 3 years develops blue-black pigmentation of the face, shins, and hard palate. The pigmentation is primarily due to:
opts: Increased melanin synthesis stimulated by the drug
Drug-melanin complex deposition in the dermis
questions.exp: Antimalarial drugs (chloroquine, hydroxychloroquine) chelate melanin and form drug-melanin complexes that are phagocytosed by dermal macrophages, causing blue-black pigmentation in sun-exposed areas. This differs from minocycline pigmentation (iron-drug complexes and melanin) and amiodarone (lipofuscin-related).

questions.q: A 35-year-old nurse with chronic hand eczema that worsens at work undergoes patch testing with the European baseline series. Which statement about patch testing is most accurate?
opts: Readings are taken only at 48 hours after patch removal
The standard baseline series contains the most prevalent contact allergens in the general population
A positive patch test reaction alone confirms clinically relevant allergic contact dermatitis
Patch testing is the gold standard for diagnosing irritant contact dermatitis
questions.exp: The European baseline (standard) series is designed to detect the most common contact allergens in the general population. Readings must be performed at 48 h AND 96 h — late readings are essential for metals (gold, cobalt) and corticosteroids. A positive test confirms sensitisation but clinical relevance must be established by history. Patch testing cannot diagnose ICD (no immunological sensitisation).

questions.q: A 20-year-old male presents with symmetrically distributed target lesions on palms, soles, and dorsum of hands following a cold sore episode 2 weeks ago. There is mild lip crusting (one mucosal site). Skin detachment is absent. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: EM minor: typical/atypical target lesions in acral distribution, involvement of at most 1 mucosal site, triggered by HSV (90% of recurrent EM), no significant epidermal detachment. EM major: typical targets + 2 or more mucosal sites. SJS: drug-triggered, atypical flat targets/macules, 2 or more mucosae, <10% BSA epidermal detachment. EM is now classified separately from SJS/TEN.

questions.q: A 28-year-old obese female presents with a 3-year history of recurrent painful nodules, abscesses, and sinus tracts in bilateral axillae and groin with scarring. Multiple antibiotic courses have given only partial relief. The primary pathophysiological mechanism of hidradenitis suppurativa is:
opts: Primary eccrine sweat gland infection leading to abscess formation
Follicular occlusion with secondary apocrine gland rupture and inflammation
Primary apocrine gland infection with Staphylococcus aureus
Sebaceous gland hyperplasia causing ductal obstruction
questions.exp: Hidradenitis suppurativa (acne inversa) is primarily a disease of follicular occlusion (keratin plug in the folliculopilosebaceous unit), not primary apocrine or eccrine infection. Occlusion leads to follicular dilatation, rupture, dermal inflammatory cascade, and secondary involvement of adjacent apocrine glands. Genetic factors (NCSTN, PSENEN mutations) and smoking/obesity are key risk factors.
